home.title: El diablo murió en Petorca
home.provinceLabel: Commune of Petorca: Pedegua · Petorca · Chincolco · Hierro Viejo
home.subtitle: The valley where the devil danced the cueca, lost his poncho and stayed for good. Old railway tunnels, petroglyphs over 800 years old, a church from 1640, chicha and country empanadas. Come and discover it… or rediscover it if you live here.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.intro: This site does not ask you to create an account or leave your name or email. Here is what does happen when you use it.

session.title: Anonymous session
session.body: If you like a place, comment or build "My trip", an anonymous session with a random identifier is created and stored in your browser. It lets us remember your trip and likes and keeps anyone else from changing them. It does not include your name, email or phone.

comments.title: Comments
comments.body: Whatever you write in a comment is stored as-is, without your name, and is only published after an administrator reviews it.

analytics.title: Usage statistics
analytics.body: We record anonymous events: which places, routes and villages are viewed, what is searched and which filters are used. We do not store who you are or your IP address. They help us learn what people are interested in across the area.

location.title: Location
location.body: Your location is only used if you turn on live navigation, and it is shown on the map on your own device.

thirdParties.title: Services we use
thirdParties.body: The site runs on Supabase (database), Vercel (hosting), Google (place photos), OpenStreetMap (street-route calculation) and a map provider. To show you that content, those services receive your browser's requests and, with them, your IP address. To prevent abuse, the server briefly counts requests per IP without storing them.

contact.title: Contact
contact.body: For questions, corrections or to ask for data to be removed, write to the site's developer (see Info).

legend.title: The legend of the Devil
legend.subtitle: Some say the devil lost his poncho here… Others say he rode in on horseback and died around here… but others say they can still feel him, and he may keep you company along the way.

saying.title: The saying
saying.body: In the valley people repeat an old saying: "The Devil died in Petorca and was buried in La Ligua." Behind it there is a poem more than 130 years old and several stories still told in the area.

poem.title: The 1894 poem
poem.body: The oldest record is "La Muerte del Diablo" (The Death of the Devil), a poem that Elías Lizana, vicar of Hierro Viejo, published in 1894 in the newspaper La Voz de Petorca. It follows the Devil's wanderings through the area: he is born in Mincha, works as a miner in the Choapa, loses his poncho in Chalaco and dies in Petorca.

versions.title: The versions people tell
versions.intro: Some collected in the book Narraciones tradicionales de Petorca y sus alrededores (2015); others from local accounts.

stranger.title: The lucky stranger
stranger.body: In the days of gold and silver, a stranger always won at cards and had a reputation as a seducer. The miners, sure he was the Devil, found the jar where he kept his winnings and killed him. In his pocket they found a little picture of the Virgin: he was not the Devil. He was buried in La Ligua. As told by Ana Leyton Morales.

rider.title: The rider and his poncho
rider.body: In a tavern in Petorca a rider in a black cape appeared, buying drinks and dancing the cueca. When he left there was a smell of sulfur and, ever since, at night a rider can be heard calling for his poncho from the hills of Chalaco.

miner.title: The miner nicknamed "The Devil"
miner.body: A miner from the Choapa, hard-working but quarrelsome, earned the nickname "The Devil". He was chased through the hills of Chalaco and died in the square of Petorca; he was buried in La Ligua.

route.title: The tourist route's version
route.body: The "Donde el Diablo perdió el poncho" tourist route tells that the Devil danced the cueca with the miners on payday, in a black tailcoat and with gold teeth; that he forgot his poncho after a New Year's party where he paid everyone's bill; and that he fled from the priests up the Devil's Staircase, whose steps run "backwards". That is where this site's Devil comes from: tailcoat, gold tooth and a poncho about to be lost.
